claim: In both vertebrates and invertebrates, commissural neurons prevent premature responsiveness to the midline repellant Slit by downregulating surface levels of its receptor Roundabout1 (Robo1).
source: In both vertebrates and invertebrates, commissural neurons prevent premature responsiveness to the midline repellant Slit by downregulating surface levels of its receptor Roundabout1 (Robo1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research (Evans et al., 2015; Keleman et al., 2002; Kinoshita-Kawada et al., 2019; Sabatier et al., 2004) as indicated in the full manuscript text.

claim: In Drosophila, Commissureless (Comm) plays a critical role in downregulating Robo1 surface levels.
source: In Drosophila, Commissureless (Comm) plays a critical role in this process
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Keleman et al., 2002; Kidd et al., 1998; Tear et al., 1996) as indicated in the full manuscript.

claim: The conserved PY motifs in the cytoplasmic domain of Comm are required to allow the ubiquitination and lysosomal degradation of Robo1.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the conserved PY motifs in the cytoplasmic domain of Comm are required allow the ubiquitination and lysosomal degradation of Robo1.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2, 4, and 5 showing ubiquitination assays, lysosomal localization, and degradation experiments.

claim: Disruption of Comm PY motifs prevents Comm from localizing to Lamp1 positive late endosomes.
source: Disruption of these motifs prevents Comm from localizing to Lamp1 positive late endosomes
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-E demonstrating colocalization analysis between Comm variants and Lamp1.

claim: Disruption of Comm PY motifs prevents Comm from promoting axon growth across the midline in vivo.
source: Disruption of these motifs prevents Comm from localizing to Lamp1 positive late endosomes and to promote axon growth across the midline in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 showing ectopic crossing assays with PY motif mutants.

claim: nedd4 mutations result in midline crossing defects in the Drosophila embryonic nerve cord.
source: Genetic analysis shows that nedd4 mutations result in midline crossing defects in the Drosophila embryonic nerve cord
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 showing crossing defects in nedd4 mutant embryos in sensitized genetic backgrounds.

claim: Midline crossing defects in nedd4 mutants can be rescued by introduction of exogenous Nedd4.
source: Genetic analysis shows that nedd4 mutations result in midline crossing defects in the Drosophila embryonic nerve cord, which can be rescued by introduction of exogenous Nedd4.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6E-F showing rescue experiments.

claim: Nedd4 incorporates into a three-member complex with Comm and Robo1 in a PY motif-dependent manner.
source: Biochemical evidence shows that Nedd4 incorporates into a three-member complex with Comm and Robo1 in a PY motif-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Nedd4 acts with Comm in the embryonic nerve cord to downregulate Robo1 levels.
source: Finally, we present genetic evidence that Nedd4 acts with Comm in the embryonic nerve cord to downregulate Robo1 levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7D-G showing Robo1 protein levels in embryos expressing Comm and Nedd4.

claim: Comm promotes midline crossing in the nerve cord by facilitating Robo1 ubiquitination by Nedd4, ultimately leading to its degradation.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that Comm promotes midline crossing in the nerve cord by facilitating Robo1 ubiquitination by Nedd4, ultimately leading to its degradation.
evidence: This is a synthesis claim supported by multiple experimental findings including ubiquitination assays (Figure 2), localization studies (Figures 4-5), and genetic interactions (Figures 6-7).

claim: Defects in midline circuit assembly can result in horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis.
source: Defects in midline circuit assembly can result in a variety of neurodevelopmental disorders (for reviews see Engle, 2010; Izzi and Charron, 2011) including horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis (Bosley et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bosley et al., 2005.

claim: Defects in midline circuit assembly can result in congenital mirror movement disorder.
source: Defects in midline circuit assembly can result in a variety of neurodevelopmental disorders (for reviews see Engle, 2010; Izzi and Charron, 2011) including horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis (Bosley et al., 2005), congenital mirror movement disorder (Depienne et al., 2011; Srour et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Depienne et al., 2011 and Srour et al., 2010.

claim: Defects in midline circuit assembly can result in autism spectrum disorder.
source: Defects in midline circuit assembly can result in a variety of neurodevelopmental disorders (for reviews see Engle, 2010; Izzi and Charron, 2011) including horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis (Bosley et al., 2005), congenital mirror movement disorder (Depienne et al., 2011; Srour et al., 2010), autism spectrum disorder (Anitha et al., 2008; Suda et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anitha et al., 2008 and Suda et al., 2011.

claim: Defects in midline circuit assembly can result in agenesis of the corpus callosum.
source: Defects in midline circuit assembly can result in a variety of neurodevelopmental disorders (for reviews see Engle, 2010; Izzi and Charron, 2011) including horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis (Bosley et al., 2005), congenital mirror movement disorder (Depienne et al., 2011; Srour et al., 2010), autism spectrum disorder (Anitha et al., 2008; Suda et al., 2011), and agenesis of the corpus callosum (Jamuar et al., 2017; Paul et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jamuar et al., 2017 and Paul et al., 2007.

claim: Pre-crossing commissural axons are initially drawn to the midline by netrin.
source: Pre-crossing commissural axons are initially drawn to the midline by several attractive ligands including netrin (Ishii et al., 1992; Mitchell et al., 1996; Serafini et al., 1996; Serafini et al., 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ishii et al., 1992; Mitchell et al., 1996; Serafini et al., 1996; Serafini et al., 1994.

claim: Pre-crossing commissural axons are initially drawn to the midline by sonic hedgehog.
source: Pre-crossing commissural axons are initially drawn to the midline by several attractive ligands including netrin (Ishii et al., 1992; Mitchell et al., 1996; Serafini et al., 1996; Serafini et al., 1994) and sonic hedgehog (Charron et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Charron et al., 2003.

claim: Upon reaching the midline, commissural axons respond to repulsive molecules such as slits and secreted semaphorins.
source: Upon reaching the midline, however, they respond to repulsive molecules such as slits and secreted semaphorins (Brose et al., 1999; Kidd et al., 1999; Zou et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brose et al., 1999; Kidd et al., 1999; Zou et al., 2000.

claim: Nerve cords of Comm mutant embryos exhibit a complete lack of midline crossing.
source: Nerve cords of Comm mutant embryos exhibit a complete lack of midline crossing (Tear et al., 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tear et al., 1996.

claim: Comm overexpression decreases Robo1 levels and induces ectopic midline crossing events.
source: while Comm overexpression decreases Robo1 levels and induces ectopic midline crossing events (Kidd et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kidd et al., 1998.

claim: Comm is thought to act by preventing newly synthesized Robo1 from reaching the growth cone membrane by binding to it and shunting it to late endosomes.
source: Based on experiments in mammalian and insect cell culture, Comm is thought to act by preventing newly synthesized Robo1 from reaching the growth cone membrane by binding to it and shunting it to late endosomes, presumably leading to its degradation (Keleman et al., 2002; Keleman et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Keleman et al., 2002 and Keleman et al., 2005.

claim: Within a conserved region of the Comm cytoplasmic domain, there are two PY motifs (PPCY and LPSY).
source: Within a conserved region of the Comm cytoplasmic domain, there are two PY motifs (PPCY and LPSY; Myat et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Myat et al., 2002.

claim: Mutation of the LPSY motif rendered Comm unable to localize Robo1 to endosomes in cell culture.
source: In a previous study, mutation of the LPSY motif rendered Comm unable to localize Robo1 to endosomes in cell culture, and unable to induce midline crossing in vivo (Keleman et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Keleman et al., 2002.

claim: PY motifs are known binding motifs for the WW-domain containing Nedd4 family of HECT ubiquitin ligases.
source: PY motifs are known binding motifs for the WW-domain containing Nedd4 family of HECT ubiquitin ligases (Kanelis et al., 2001; Kasanov et al., 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kanelis et al., 2001 and Kasanov et al., 2001.

claim: Nedd4 ubiquitinated Comm.
source: The first study demonstrated that Nedd4 ubiquitinated Comm, and that Comm required both its PY motifs and its cytoplasmic ubiquitin-accepting lysines to direct Robo1 to endosomes and downregulate its surface expression in cell culture (Myat et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Myat et al., 2002.

claim: An un-ubiquitinatable Comm mutant (Comm KR) was indistinguishable from wild-type Comm in its ability to localize itself and Robo1 to endosomes in vitro.
source: Interestingly, in the second study, an un-ubiquitinatable Comm mutant (Comm KR with all ubiquitin-accepting lysines mutated to arginines) was undistinguishable from wild-type Comm in its ability to localize itself and Robo1 to endosomes in vitro and induce Comm gain-of-function phenotypes in vivo (Keleman et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Keleman et al., 2005.

claim: Embryos homozygous for a chromosomal deletion that removes Nedd-4 had no noticeable defects in commissural axon guidance when stained with a pan-neuronal marker.
source: When stained with a pan-neuronal marker, embryos homozygous for a chromosomal deletion that removes Nedd-4 had no noticeable defects in commissural axon guidance (Keleman et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Keleman et al., 2005.

claim: Mutating the Comm LPSY motif alone does not completely disrupt proper localization to late endosomes in vitro and in vivo.
source: In contrast to previous literature, we find that mutating the Comm LPSY motif alone does not completely disrupt proper localization to late endosomes in vitro and in vivo
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5 showing localization of Comm 1PY mutant.

claim: Mutating the Comm LPSY motif alone does not completely disrupt direction of Robo1 away from the cell surface.
source: In contrast to previous literature, we find that mutating the Comm LPSY motif alone does not completely disrupt proper localization to late endosomes in vitro and in vivo, direction of Robo1 away from the cell surface
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing Robo1 localization with Comm 1PY.

claim: Mutating the Comm LPSY motif alone does not completely disrupt promotion of midline crossing.
source: In contrast to previous literature, we find that mutating the Comm LPSY motif alone does not completely disrupt proper localization to late endosomes in vitro and in vivo, direction of Robo1 away from the cell surface, and promotion of midline crossing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1 showing that Comm 1PY can still induce some ectopic crossing.

claim: PY motifs are necessary for Comm to facilitate Robo1 ubiquitination and lysosomal degradation.
source: In addition, while previous studies only assayed the ubiquitination of Comm itself, we demonstrate that PY motifs are necessary for Comm to facilitate Robo1 ubiquitination and lysosomal degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2D-E showing ubiquitination assays.

claim: Loss of Nedd4, but not Smurf or Su(dx), leads to midline crossing defects in the embryonic nerve cord.
source: Using sensitized genetic backgrounds, we provide evidence that loss of Nedd4, but not Smurf or Su(dx), lead to midline crossing defects in the embryonic nerve cord.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 and Figure 6 supplements 2 and 3 showing genetic analysis of Nedd4 family members.

claim: Comm, Robo1, and Nedd4 interact as a three-member complex.
source: In addition, we observe that Comm, Robo1, and Nedd4 interact as a three-member complex
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Comm PY motifs are necessary for Nedd4 incorporation into the Comm-Robo1 complex.
source: In addition, we observe that Comm, Robo1, and Nedd4 interact as a three-member complex and that Comm PY motifs are necessary for Nedd4 incorporation into this complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7A-B showing reduced Nedd4 binding with PY mutants.

claim: Exogenous Nedd4 enhances the ability of Comm to downregulate Robo1 protein levels in vivo.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that exogenous Nedd4 enhances the ability of Comm to downregulate Robo1 protein levels in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 7D-G showing Robo1 levels with Comm and Nedd4 co-expression.

claim: Comm acts as a substrate adapter to bring Robo1 into proximity to Nedd4, which it recruits via its PY motifs.
source: Taken together, these findings support a model in which Comm acts as a substrate adaptor to bring Robo1 into proximity to Nedd4, which it recruits via its PY motifs.
evidence: This is a model claim supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including complex formation (Figure 7A-B) and functional assays (Figures 1-7).

claim: Nedd4 ubiquitinates Robo1, shunting it away from the growth cone membrane and to late endosomes and lysosomes for degradation.
source: This adaptor activity then allows Nedd4 to ubiquitinate Robo1, shunting it away from the growth cone membrane and to late endosomes and lysosomes for degradation.
evidence: This is a model claim supported by ubiquitination data (Figure 2), localization data (Figures 4-5), and degradation assays (Figures 2-3).

claim: Downregulation of Robo1 surface levels renders commissural axons insensitive to repulsive slit signals, allowing for midline crossing.
source: Finally, the resulting downregulation of Robo1 surface levels renders commissural axons insensitive to repulsive slit signals, allowing for midline crossing.
evidence: This is a model claim based on established knowledge about Robo1 function and the experimental data showing Robo1 downregulation correlates with midline crossing.

claim: WT Comm induced ectopic FasII crossing in roughly half the commissures in the nerve cord (mean = 52%, n=17).
source: We found that WT Comm induced ectopic FAS II crossing in roughly half the commissures in the nerve cord (mean = 52%, n=17).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative data from the experiment shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Comm 1PY was able to induce ectopic FasII crossing, although it was significantly less effective than WT (p<0.0001, ANOVA/Tukey, n=23).
source: Comm 1PY was also able to induce ectopic FAS II crossing, although it was significantly less effective than WT (p<0.0001, ANOVA/Tukey, n=23).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis from the experiment shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Nerve cords of embryos expressing Comm 2PY were indistinguishable from those of control embryos not carrying any Comm transgenes (p=0.997, ANOVA/Tukey, 2PY n=20, CTRL n=18).
source: Finally, nerve cords of embryos expressing Comm 2PY were indistinguishable from those of control embryos not carrying any Comm transgenes (p=0.997, ANOVA/Tukey, 2PY n=20, CTRL n=18; Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis from the experiment shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Nearly all nerve cord segments of embryos expressing WT Comm had ectopic apterous crossing events (mean = 85.28%, n=29).
source: Nearly all nerve cord segments of embryos expressing WT Comm had ectopic apterous crossing events (mean = 85.28%, n=29).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative data from the experiment shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Comm 1PY induced significantly fewer ectopic apterous crossing events than WT.
source: Consistent with our FasII data, Comm 1PY induced significantly fewer ectopic crossing events than WT
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative data from the experiment shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Comm 2PY was completely unable to induce ectopic apterous crossing.
source: Consistent with our FasII data, Comm 1PY induced significantly fewer ectopic crossing events than WT, and Comm 2PY was completely unable to induce ectopic crossing (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative data from the experiment shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Pan-neural expression of 10 X Comm-2PY leads to a striking gain of function phenotype where many segments display strong ectopic crossing.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that pan-neural expression of 10 X Comm-2PY, which has no effect when expressed at lower levels, leads to a striking gain of function phenotype where many segments display strong ectopic crossing, both with FasII and with HRP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Co-expression of WT comm significantly reduces Robo1 levels compared to those in cells transfected with Robo1 alone.
source: We found that co-expression of WT comm significantly reduces Robo1 levels compared to those in cells transfected with Robo1 alone (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Comm 1PY reduces Robo1 levels, though it is significantly less effective at doing so than WT Comm.
source: Comm 1PY also reduces Robo1 levels, though it is significantly less effective at doing so than WT Comm
evidence: This claim is directly supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Comm 2PY is completely unable to reduce Robo1 levels.
source: while Comm 2PY is completely unable to reduce Robo1 levels (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Mutating the PY motifs in Comm increases the stability of Comm protein.
source: Interestingly, mutating the PY motifs in Comm also affects stability of the Comm protein itself. Levels of Comm 1PY and 2PY are elevated relative to WT Comm (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: WT Comm significantly increases Robo1 ubiquitination levels relative to those observed in cells transfected with Robo1 alone.
source: WT Comm significantly increases Robo1 ubiquitination levels relative to those observed in cells transfected with Robo1 alone
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Removing either LPSY or both PY motifs eliminates Comm's ability to enhance Robo1 ubiquitination.
source: WT Comm significantly increases Robo1 ubiquitination levels relative to those observed in cells transfected with Robo1 alone and removing either LPSY or both PY motifs eliminates Comm's ability to enhance Robo1 ubiquitination (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: In cells co-transfected with Robo1 and WT Comm, treatment with the lysosomal inhibitor chloroquine significantly stabilizes ubiquitinated Robo1.
source: Importantly, in cells co-transfected with Robo1 and WT Comm, treatment with the lysosomal inhibitor chloroquine significantly stabilizes ubiquitinated Robo1 (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunoprecipitation data with chloroquine treatment shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Comm facilitates Robo1 ubiquitination in a PY motif-dependent manner and this ubiquitinated Robo1 is degraded in the lysosome.
source: Taken together, our results show that Comm facilitates Robo1 ubiquitination in a PY motif-dependent manner and this ubiquitinated Robo1 is degraded in the lysosome.
evidence: This is a synthesis claim supported by the ubiquitination and chloroquine treatment data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Overexpression of WT comm under the elavGal4 driver significantly reduces endogenous Robo1 levels.
source: Overexpression of WT comm under the elavGal4 driver significantly reduces endogenous Robo1 levels (Figure 3Aii, B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Loss of one PY motif significantly diminished Comm's ability to downregulate Robo1 levels.
source: As predicted from our in vitro data, loss of one PY motif significantly diminished Comm's ability to downregulate Robo1 levels
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Loss of both PY motifs eliminated Comm's ability to downregulate Robo1 levels and endogenous Robo1 levels are indistinguishable from control embryos.
source: while loss of both eliminated the ability altogether and endogenous Robo1 levels are indistinguishable from control embryos (Figure 3Aii, B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Expression of 10 X UAS Comm 2PY does not reduce endogenous Robo1 levels at all.
source: Intriguingly, while expression of either 10 X UAS Comm WT or Comm 1PY leads to even stronger reduction in endogenous Robo1 than the 5 X transgenes, expression of 10 X UAS Comm 2PY does not reduce endogenous Robo1 levels at all (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Loss of PY motifs increases Comm levels in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We also tested the effects of mutating the PY motifs on the expression of the Comm protein itself, and consistent with our in vitro experiments, we find that loss of PY motifs increases Comm levels in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 3A and C.

claim: Even when over-expressed using the Gal4-UAS system, Comm (both 5 X and 10 X UAS) is barely detected unless the PY motifs are mutated.
source: Interestingly, even when over-expressed using the Gal4-UAS system, Comm (both 5 X and 10 X UAS) is barely detected unless the PY motifs are mutated.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In cells transfected with Robo1 alone, Robo1 is diffusely localized throughout the cell, in intracellular puncta, and at the cell surface.
source: In cells transfected with Robo1 alone, Robo1 is diffusely localized throughout the cell, in intracellular puncta, and at the cell surface (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When co-transfected with WT Comm, Robo1 is predominantly found with Comm in intracellular puncta.
source: As observed in previous studies (Keleman et al., 2002; Keleman et al., 2005; Myat et al., 2002), when co-transfected with WT Comm, we see a dramatic change in Robo1 localization. Instead of diffuse localization throughout the cell, Robo1 is predominantly found with Comm in intracellular puncta (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A-B and is consistent with prior citations.

claim: Disruption of the LPSY motif alone (Comm 1PY) does not alter Comm localization compared to WT.
source: In contrast to previous findings (Keleman et al., 2002), disruption of the LPSY motif alone (Comm 1PY) does not alter Comm localization compared to WT
evidence: This claim is directly supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Comm 1PY is significantly less effective at routing Robo1 to intracellular puncta.
source: however, Comm 1PY is significantly less effective at routing Robo1 to intracellular puncta, and we observe a return of diffuse Robo1 expression (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Comm2PY shows diffuse localization throughout the cell, as well as impaired ability to route Robo1 to intracellular puncta.
source: In contrast to Comm 1PY, Comm2PY shows diffuse localization throughout the cell, as well as impaired ability to route Robo1 to intracellular puncta.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: In control embryos, Robo1 is present on the surface of longitudinal portions of axons in the developing ventral nerve cord.
source: In control embryos, Robo1 is present on the surface of longitudinal portions of axons in the developing ventral nerve cord (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by surface staining data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Minimal Robo1 is detected on the axonal surface in embryos expressing 5 X UAS wild-type Comm.
source: In contrast, minimal Robo1 is detected on the axonal surface in embryos expressing 5 X UAS wild-type Comm (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by surface staining data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In embryos expressing 5 X UAS Comm 2PY, Robo1 is expressed normally on the axonal surface.
source: In embryos expressing 5 X UAS Comm 2PY, Robo1 is expressed normally on the axonal surface.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by surface staining data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: 10 X UAS WT Comm is restricted to cell bodies and displays a punctate expression pattern indicative of localization in intracellular vesicles.
source: We found that 10 X UAS WT Comm is restricted to cell bodies and displays a punctate expression pattern indicative of localization in intracellular vesicles (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: 10 X UAS Comm 1PY is observed in cell body puncta and is also present in axons.
source: Like WT Comm, 10 X UAS Comm 1PY is observed in cell body puncta. However, Comm 1PY, unlike WT Comm, is also present in axons.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: 10 X UAS Comm 2PY displays even greater enrichment in axons than Comm 1PY.
source: 10 X UAS Comm 2PY displays even greater enrichment in axons (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: When Robo1 is co-expressed with 10 X UAS Comm, its expression pattern mimics that of the Comm variant with which it is expressed.
source: When Robo1 is co-expressed with 10 X UAS Comm, its expression pattern mimics that of the Comm variant with which it is expressed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: When co-expressed with WT Comm, Robo1 expression is absent from axons and restricted to the cell body, often in Comm-positive intracellular puncta.
source: Notably, when co-expressed with WT Comm, Robo1 expression is absent from axons and restricted to the cell body, often in Comm-positive intracellular puncta.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Robo1 co-expressed with PY mutant Comm variants can be found alongside these Comm variants in axons.
source: Meanwhile, Robo1 co-expressed with PY mutant Comm variants can be found alongside these Comm variants in axons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Robo co-localizes equally with WT and PY mutant Comm variants in vivo.
source: Robo co-localizes equally with WT and PY mutant Comm variants in vivo (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Both Comm PY mutant variants show a significant reduction in total co-localization with Rab7 and Lamp1 relative to wild-type Comm.
source: Each Comm variant can be observed in puncta positive for Rab7 or Lamp1 (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2); however, both Comm PY mutant variants show a significant reduction in total co-localization with these late endosomal and lysosomal markers relative to wild-type Comm (Figure 5C–E, p<0.05 for both 1PY and 2PY, ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 5C-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: PY mutant Comm variants show significantly less co-localization with Lamp1 even when only observing Comm present in cell bodies.
source: Interestingly, PY mutant Comm variants show significantly less co-localization with Lamp1 even when only observing Comm present in cell bodies, suggesting that with Lamp1, total co-localization is not only decreased due to Comm leakage into axons, but also due to compromised routing to the correct subcellular compartments within cell bodies (Figure 5C and E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 5C and E.

claim: Nedd4 protein is strongly enriched in the ventral nerve cord of stage 14 embryos.
source: Using this tool, we observe a strong enrichment of Nedd4 protein in the ventral nerve cord of stage 14 embryos, a stage when many commissural axons are extending across the midline.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nedd4 is present in both cell bodies and CNS axons.
source: Using this line, we are able to detect Nedd4 protein in both cell bodies and CNS axons, indicating that Nedd4 is present at the right time and place to play a role in commissural axon guidance (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Embryos homozygous for the Nedd4T119FS loss of function allele showed no obvious defects when examined with HRP immunofluorescence.
source: When we examined embryos homozygous for this loss of function allele with HRP immunofluorescence, we detected no obvious defects (Figure 6A), consistent prior observations using a chromosomal deletion for Nedd4 (Keleman et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6A and is consistent with prior citation.

claim: Removing one copy of Nedd4 does not increase crossing defects in the fra-null background, as measured by commissure thickness with HRP.
source: While removing one copy of Nedd4 does not increase crossing defects in the fra-null background, as measured by commissure thickness with HRP (Figure 6A and B)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Removing both copies of Nedd4 leads to a significant enhancement of the fra mutant phenotype, and a profound disruption in midline crossing.
source: removing both copies of Nedd4 leads to a significant enhancement of the fra mutant phenotype, and a profound disruption in midline crossing, in some instances resembling comm loss of function mutants (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: fra, nedd4 double mutant embryos are missing over half of their commissures (compared to the <10% missing in fra single mutants).
source: fra, nedd4 double mutant embryos are missing over half of their commissures (compared to the <10% missing in fra single mutants) and most of the remaining commissures are thin (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Nedd4 homozygous mutants display significantly increased EW non-crossing phenotypes in the Fra∆C background.
source: While Nedd4 heterozygotes show no alterations in commissural axon guidance defects in the Fra∆C background, Nedd4 homozygous mutants display significantly increased EW non-crossing phenotypes.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: Expressing a UAS Nedd4 transgene in embryos homozygous mutant for nedd4 in the Fra∆C background leads to a significant reduction in the non-crossing defects.
source: We find that expressing a UAS Nedd4 transgene in embryos homozygous mutant for nedd4 in the Fra∆C background leads to a significant reduction in the non-crossing defects (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: Nedd4 functions cell autonomously in neurons.
source: We find that expressing a UAS Nedd4 transgene in embryos homozygous mutant for nedd4 in the Fra∆C background leads to a significant reduction in the non-crossing defects (Figure 6E and F). Taken together, these results demonstrate an important role for Nedd4 in promoting midline crossing and suggest that it functions cell autonomously in neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiment where neuron-specific expression of Nedd4 rescues the phenotype, shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: Su(Dx) is expressed broadly or ubiquitously throughout all stages of embryogenesis including in the nerve cord of stages 14 through 16 embryos.
source: Data reported for Su(Dx) show that it is expressed broadly or ubiquitously throughout all stages of embryogenesis including in the nerve cord of stages 14 through 16 embryos.
evidence: This claim is based on data from the Berkeley Drosophila Genome Project database.

claim: Smurf is broadly expressed during embryogenesis, including in the developing nerve cord.
source: No data is publicly available for Smurf, so we generated our own in situ probes to visualize the Smurf embryonic mRNA expression pattern and found that like Su(Dx), Smurf is broadly expressed during embryogenesis, including in the developing nerve cord (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Zygotic loss of either Smurf or Su(dx) function produced no visible midline crossing defects in nerve cords stained with the pan-neuronal marker HRP.
source: Similar to nedd4 mutants, zygotic loss of either Smurf or Su(dx) function produced no visible midline crossing defects in nerve cords stained with the pan-neuronal marker HRP (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6 and supplements.

claim: Removing both zygotic copies of either smurf or su(dx) does not increase the occurrence of EW non-crossing in either fra mutant embryos or in embryos expressing Fra∆C using egGal4.
source: In marked contrast to our findings with nedd4, removing both zygotic copies of either smurf or su(dx) does not increase the occurrence of EW non-crossing in either fra mutant embryos or in embryos expressing Fra∆C using egGal4 (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-F and Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6 supplements 2 and 3.

claim: When Robo1 and Nedd4 are co-transfected in the absence of Comm, very little if any association between Nedd4 and Robo1 is detected.
source: When Robo1 and Nedd4 are co-transfected in the absence of Comm, we detect very little if any association between Nedd4 and Robo1 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: When Robo1, Nedd4, and Comm are all expressed, Nedd4 readily co-precipitates with Robo1.
source: Strikingly, when all three proteins are expressed, Nedd4 readily co-precipitates with Robo1, even though the presence of Comm greatly reduces Robo1 protein levels (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Mutating the PY motifs leads to a significant decrease in the amount of Nedd4 that is incorporated into the Robo1-Comm complex.
source: As predicted, mutating the PY motifs leads to a significant decrease in the amount of Nedd4 that is incorporated into the complex, even though the level of Robo1 protein expression increases when Comm PY motifs are mutated (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: In lysate of embryos co-expressing 10 X UAS WT Comm and 10 X UAS Nedd4, a complex consisting of these two proteins and endogenous Robo1 can be immunoprecipitated.
source: To determine whether Nedd4 can function together with Comm in vivo to downregulate the expression of the Robo1 receptor, we first investigated whether Robo1, Comm, and Nedd4 could form a three-member complex like that we observed in cells, and found that in lysate of embryos co-expressing 10 X UAS WT Comm and 10 X UAS Nedd4, we were able to immunoprecipitate a complex consisting of these two proteins and endogenous Robo1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pan-neural expression of Comm leads to a striking reduction in Robo1 protein levels.
source: As predicted from our in vitro measurements of the effect of Comm on Robo1 expression levels, pan-neural expression of Comm leads to a striking reduction in Robo1 protein levels.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D-E.

claim: The effect of Comm on Robo1 protein levels is significantly enhanced in embryos co-expressing Comm and Nedd4.
source: Importantly this effect is significantly enhanced in embryos co-expressing Comm and Nedd4 (Figure 7D and E)
evidence: This claim is directly supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D-E.

claim: Co-expression of Nedd4 and Comm leads to reduced levels of Comm protein relative to embryos expressing Comm alone.
source: Interestingly, and consistent with our in vitro biochemistry, co-expression of Nedd4 and Comm also leads to reduced levels of Comm protein relative to embryos expressing Comm alone, suggesting that Comm, like Robo1 is likely degraded due to ubiquitination from Nedd4 (Figure 7E, see discussion).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Axonal Robo1 levels are further reduced when Nedd4 is co-expressed with Comm compared to Comm alone.
source: Consistent with the data presented in earlier (Figure 3 with accompanying supplement, and 4), ectopic expression of 5 X UAS Comm results in a striking decrease in axonal Robo1 expression. Importantly, axonal Robo1 levels are further reduced when Nedd4 is co-expressed with Comm (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 7F-G.

claim: Nedd4 enhances reduction of nerve cord width induced by overexpression of Comm.
source: These findings demonstrate that Nedd4 can enhance reduction of nerve cord width induced by overexpression of Comm.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Nedd4 enhances the severity of morphological defects (segment collapse) induced by Comm overexpression.
source: The presence of this 'complete collapse' phenotypic class demonstrates that addition of Nedd4 enhances the severity of morphological defects induced by Comm overexpression.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Nedd4 enhances the Comm gain-of function phenotype defined by ectopic crossing, likely by enhancing downregulation of Robo1 levels.
source: Taken together with our nerve cord width data, these findings show that Nedd4 enhances the Comm gain-of function phenotype defined by ectopic crossing, likely by enhancing downregulation of Robo1 levels.
evidence: This is a synthesis claim supported by multiple morphological measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the absence of its PY motifs, Comm can still inhibit midline repulsion and this effect is not due to reduced levels of Robo1 protein.
source: In addition, our observation that expression of 10 X UAS Comm 2PY does not reduce endogenous Robo1 levels suggests that in the absence of its PY motifs, Comm can still inhibit midline repulsion and that this effect is not due to reduced levels of Robo1 protein (see Discussion).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 10X Comm 2PY causes ectopic crossing (Figure 1 supplement 1) but does not reduce Robo1 levels (Figure 3 supplement 1).

claim: The LPSY motif is dispensable for proper Comm localization in cell culture but is required for effective routing of Robo1.
source: In summary, the LPSY motif is dispensable for proper Comm localization in cell culture but is required for effective routing of Robo1, while loss of both PY motifs, causes Comm mis-localization as well as a failure to recruit Robo1 to intracellular puncta.
evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on the localization data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Loss of both PY motifs causes Comm mis-localization as well as a failure to recruit Robo1 to intracellular puncta.
source: In summary, the LPSY motif is dispensable for proper Comm localization in cell culture but is required for effective routing of Robo1, while loss of both PY motifs, causes Comm mis-localization as well as a failure to recruit Robo1 to intracellular puncta.
evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on the localization data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The primary site of Comm function is in the cell soma.
source: The observation that mutating Comm PY motifs leads to 'leakage' of both Comm and Robo1 into axons, coupled with a failure of these mutants to down-regulate Robo1 and promote midline crossing strongly suggest that the primary site of Comm function is in the cell soma.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PY mutants leak into axons and lose function, suggesting the soma is where Comm normally acts.

claim: Most actively degradative intracellular compartments are restricted to the soma in neurons.
source: As most actively degradative intracellular compartments are restricted to the soma in neurons (for a review of the neuronal endolysosomal system, see Roney et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Roney et al., 2022.

claim: Ndfip1 and Ndfip2 share sequence similarity to the region of Comm containing PY motifs.
source: Among these proteins that may function analogously to Comm, the Nedd4 family interacting proteins Ndfip1 and Ndfip2 share sequence similarity to the region of Comm containing PY motifs and appear to act as its functional analog in mice.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Ndfip proteins.

claim: Loss of mammalian Ndfip proteins impedes effective midline crossing and results in the upregulation of Robo1 levels in pre-crossing commissural axons in the spinal cord.
source: Like Comm, loss of mammalian Ndfip proteins impedes effective midline crossing and results in the upregulation of Robo1 levels in pre-crossing commissural axons in the spinal cord.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Gorla et al., 2019).

claim: Ndfip proteins negatively regulate Robo1 expression by facilitating Robo1 ubiquitination, diversion away from the cell surface, trafficking to late endosomes, and ultimately, degradation.
source: In addition, Ndfip proteins negatively regulate Robo1 expression in a manner nearly identical to that of Comm: by facilitating Robo1 ubiquitination, diversion away from the cell surface, trafficking to late endosomes, and ultimately, degradation (Gorla et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gorla et al., 2019.

claim: Only the Nedd4 homologs Nedd4-1 and Nedd4-2, and the Su(dx) homolog WWP2 can enhance Robo1 ubiquitination and degradation in mammals.
source: While the seven E3 ligases most related to Drosophila Nedd4 family members can all bind Ndfip proteins in vitro, only the Nedd4 homologs Nedd4-1 and Nedd4-2, and the Su(dx) homolog WWP2 can enhance Robo1 ubiquitination and degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Gorla et al., 2022).

claim: Smurf homologs Smurf1 and Smurf2 can bind to Ndfip proteins in the absence of functional PY motifs.
source: Unlike the other Nedd4 family ligases tested, Smurf homologs Smurf1 and Smurf2 can bind to Ndfip proteins in the absence of functional PY motifs suggesting that they bind to additional structural elements of Ndfip proteins and may be involved in different biological processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Gorla et al., 2022).

claim: Single and double conditional knockouts of Nedd4-1 and Nedd4-2 display impaired axon guidance across the floor plate of the spinal cord.
source: In addition, single and double conditional knockouts of Nedd4-1 and Nedd4- 2 display impaired axon guidance across the floor plate of the spinal cord.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Gorla et al., 2022).

claim: Mammalian Nedd4 homologs play an important role in commissural axon guidance in the spinal cord.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate an important role for mammalian Nedd4 homologs in commissural axon guidance in the spinal cord (Gorla et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gorla et al., 2022.

claim: The same cargo can be ubiquitinated by different E3 ligases in different cellular contexts.
source: These additional factors appear to be highly cell-type specific, as the same cargo can be ubiquitinated by different E3 ligases in different cellular contexts.
evidence: This is supported by examples cited in the text about DMT1 ubiquitination.

claim: Ndfip-mediated ubiquitylation of DMT1 is catalyzed by Nedd4-2 in neuronal cells.
source: For example, Ndfip-mediated ubiquitylation of the divalent metal ion transporter (DMT1) is catalyzed by Nedd4-2 in neuronal cells (Howitt et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Howitt et al., 2009.

claim: Ndfip-mediated ubiquitylation of DMT1 is catalyzed by WWP2 in other non-neuronal cell types.
source: For example, Ndfip-mediated ubiquitylation of the divalent metal ion transporter (DMT1) is catalyzed by Nedd4-2 in neuronal cells (Howitt et al., 2009), but is catalyzed by WWP2 in other non-neuronal cell types (Foot et al., 2008; Gorla et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Foot et al., 2008 and Gorla et al., 2022.

claim: In both vertebrates and invertebrates, Nedd4 substrate adaptor proteins serve as a vital means of downregulating growth cone Robo1 levels by facilitating Robo1 ubiquitination, trafficking to lysosomes, and ultimately, degradation.
source: In both vertebrates and invertebrates, Nedd4 substrate adaptor proteins serve as a vital means of downregulating growth cone Robo1 levels by facilitating Robo1 ubiquitination, trafficking to lysosomes, and ultimately, degradation.
evidence: This is a synthesis claim based on the findings in this study and prior work in mammals.
